title: Case study: URL shortener

kcs.statement: Base62 encoding with 7 characters gives 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion distinct short codes, enough for about 1,000 new URLs per second for over 100 years.

A key generation service guarantees that short codes are unique, not that they are unpredictable: codes from counter ranges come out in sequence, so anyone can guess them. When codes must be non-guessable, the service pre-generates codes from a cryptographically secure random source. Each code must be long enough that guessing a valid one is impractical. Each code is stored under a uniqueness constraint (an atomic insert-if-absent that retries on a collision), and then the code is handed out exactly once.

A 301 (permanent) redirect is cacheable by default, so browsers and proxies may serve repeat clicks without reaching the service. A 302 is not cached by default but can be when caching headers allow it, so a shortener that must count every click returns a 302 with Cache-Control: no-store (or private, max-age=0) rather than relying on the status code alone.
Redirect traffic is read-heavy (often around 100:1). A cache-aside cache holding the hottest ~20% of mappings in front of a key-value store sharded by short code serves most redirects.

problem_ideas: With 100M new URLs a month and 500 bytes per row, estimate storage over 5 years.
How many base62 characters do you need for 50 billion URLs? Show the log.
Two app servers hash the same long URL with MD5 and truncate it to 7 characters. Walk through the collision and how a key generation service avoids it.
The marketing team wants click counts per link. Choose the redirect status and the Cache-Control header that keep repeat clicks visible, and say what a 301 would cost.
Size a redirect cache for 20K reads/s using the 80/20 rule and 500-byte entries.
Design expiry cleanup for links with a TTL without scanning the whole table at peak hours.
